items.title: PRAY: 24-Year-Old Youth Pastor Dies Running Portland Marathon
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: A youth pastor died after rounding one of the miles of the Portland Marathon on Sunday. Treyton “Trey” Lara, 24, […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A youth pastor died after rounding one of the miles of the Portland Marathon on Sunday.

Treyton “Trey” Lara, 24, reportedly collapsed just before mile 20 of the marathon, right after slowing down briefly to give his wife, Audrey Shin-Lara, a kiss between miles 18 and 19.

“He ran over, was able to give me a kiss, was smiling, and then ran off,” she told local Portland news outlet KGW-TV. “He looked good. And then so I drove off to the finish line, where the rest of our family and friends were going to watch him finish.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Trey Lara (@treytonlara)

Audrey, 24, had been moving with him the entire race. She first stopped to cheer him on at mile 10, then mile 14, then mile 18, and was headed to the end to celebrate all together.

The now-grieving wife said Trey had been training for months and showed no signs of distress of health issues at all, describing running as something her husband did to “relax and release.”

Soon after loading into the car to head to the finish line, Audrey said her mother-in-law called her, telling her Trey had collapsed around mile 20 and that first responders were performing CPR on him. He was transported to a nearby hospital but, by that point, doctors said it was too late.

“We’re all still in a little bit of shock,” said Audrey. “We tried going to bed and we’re like, ‘We’re gonna wake up and it’ll be a really bad dream. And he’ll be right there.'”

While they were married for just under five years, Audrey told reporters they first met one another at 12 years old. She called her late husband “one of one.”

“We met at a summer camp,” she remembered. “He saw me, and I guess he told his friends and even his best friend’s mom, he said, ‘That’s the girl I’m going to marry.’ And I didn’t actually believe it, but now I want to believe it.”

Camp was clearly a major theme in the Laras’ lives.

The couple had just launched a youth summer camp of their own, Camp Genesis, this past summer.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Trey Lara (@treytonlara)

“[I]t was just this dream that he had,” Audrey said of the nascent ministry. “He was the biggest dreamer but it wasn’t just like, ‘I’m going to do this,’ but he’s like, ‘I will do this,’ and we got it done.”

Loved ones set up a GoFundMe campaign to raise money as the family walks through this difficult time. The account describes Trey as a man whose “confidence was unshakable and his faith unwavering.”

“His faith was his defining feature,” it states. “It has spoken the loudest to those who knew him, whether they spent years with him, months with him, or even just a single day. They recognized that Trey’s faith and passion for advancing the Kingdom of God were at the center of his life.”

“He was devoted to his family and friends,” it continues. “He loved his wife, Audrey, from the moment he met her. His sisters, Jaylah and Sylvia, had the best role model in an older brother, and his parents, Omar and Misty, had the most devoted son. The man Trey became directly reflected the values they instilled in him.”

The purpose of the campaign, it notes, is to provide for Audrey’s immediate needs in the wake of her husband’s death.

Please pray for the Laras and all those impacted by this loss.

items.title: Are Angels, Demons, and Miracles REAL? Why the Supernatural Matters
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "It's easy to be embarrassed when we should actually just lean into [it]."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian apologist Gavin Ortlund’s journey toward sharing the Gospel online began during a season of “angst,” uncertainty, and questions.

“I’ve actually been through two seasons like that, where I was just asking questions of, ‘How do I know for sure?'” he said. “I know Christ. I experience Him, but I have questions coming at me, and I wanna think through the answers.”

Ortlund said that, through these experiences, God gave him a real passion for other people and a heart to try to help people coping with doubt. Unfortunately, he said, too many people don’t see the church as a place where they can find help navigating doubts.

“So they just kinda keep it quiet and don’t talk about it,” he said. “So I just want to pastor people who are going through their own doubts. I long for non-Christians to come to know Christ.”

Ortlund said reasoning is a way to help people see the truth, but the Holy Spirit must lead the conversation. When it comes to apologetics tools, he said the supernatural is actually a powerful opportunity to help people see the Lord.

“I used to think that the weird parts of the Bible were a kind of liability that we needed to make up for with these more robust arguments to get people to sort of convince them to accept the weird things,” Ortlund said. “And I wouldn’t have worded it like that … but that’s how I was functioning and, I think, over time, I’ve come to see sometimes the weird parts are themselves an asset that we can lead off with.”

He continued, “And by ‘weird,’ you know, the supernatural — angels and demons, for example, God’s miraculous healing of people, … things like that.”

Rather than feel shame or remain silent on miracles and the supernatural, he encouraged people to lean in.

“It’s easy to be embarrassed when we should actually just lean into [it],” Ortlund said. “If we believe in the Scriptures, then we have to believe in a God who intervenes in history, and He heals people, and He supernaturally bestows His Holy Spirit in a way that none of us can understand.”

Seeing darkness leave a person or showcasing the power of a miracle can actually help point people to the Gospel in a palpable way. Ortlund said there’s consistency when it comes to how God acted in the Bible and how he still behaves today.

“If we believe in the Gospels, then we have to believe that Jesus has the power to heal and is willing to heal,” he said. “Think of the man who says, ‘If you are willing, you can make me clean,'” he said. “And Jesus has a heart of compassion for people. I think when people come sincerely to Christ, and they’re laying aside their pride, and they’re just asking for help, I think the heart of Christ is compassion, and He says to that person, ‘I am willing.'”

Ortlund continued, “I believe the heart of Christ has not changed. He’s still compassionate.”

items.title: Caring About Justice Isn’t an Optional Part of Following Jesus
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Today, Reject Apathy returns to RELEVANT. Every Thursday from here on, we’ll be publishing a new story about an issue of justice and human dignity: reported carefully, told through the people living it, with real ways for you to respond. If the name is new to you, Reject Apathy has been part of RELE
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Today, Reject Apathy returns to RELEVANT.

Every Thursday from here on, we’ll be publishing a new story about an issue of justice and human dignity: reported carefully, told through the people living it, with real ways for you to respond.

If the name is new to you, Reject Apathy has been part of RELEVANT’s DNA for almost 20 years. It started with a trip to Africa I took to 2008 with Rick Warren, who became a mentor in shaping how we think and talk about these things. That trip opened my eyes, and countless trips to the frontlines since have left me with a gnawing question:

How do we reject apathy in our own lives and tangibly be the hands and feet of Christ, addressing the things closest to His heart?

That question became a website, then a section of our print magazine, then a magazine of its own. In its first issue, we wrote that Reject Apathy was “borne out of that desire to live out true compassion and to embrace justice the right way.”

That desire hasn’t changed. The world has, and so has the generation reading this. So before the first story runs, I want to tell you what we believe and why we think this matters more now than it ever has.

Apathy is the easy road

Most of us don’t willfully turn a blind eye to the world’s injustices. We have good intentions. If anything, this generation has the opposite problem from the one we had when Reject Apathy began. Back then, the challenge was awareness. Most people in church had barely heard the term “human trafficking.” Now we’re aware of everything, all the time. Every crisis on earth arrives in the same feed as the memes and the ads, and then it scrolls away.

That kind of exposure doesn’t produce compassion. It produces numbness. We feel a flash of grief, we don’t know what to do with it, and we keep moving. Do that enough times and something in us learns to stop feeling it at all.

That’s apathy. It isn’t hatred, and it usually isn’t even indifference. It’s the slow drift into a life that’s centered on ourselves because everything else feels too big.

Rejecting it is a decision. As we wrote years ago, it’s “the about-face to the gravitational pull of self-centeredness.”

Why this is a faith issue

Here is the conviction underneath everything we’ll publish: Justice is not an add-on to Christianity. It isn’t a political hobby for a certain kind of Christian. It’s a direct outgrowth of what we say we believe about God and about people.

Start at the beginning. Genesis 1:27 says every human being is made in the image of God. Not just the people who look like us, vote like us or live near us. The refugee, the unborn child, the mother without a clinic, the kid in a war zone. Each one carries what we once called God’s “divine thumbprint.” If that’s true, then what happens to them matters to Him. And if it matters to Him, it’s supposed to matter to us.

Then look at how Jesus described His own mission. When He stood up in the synagogue to announce what He had come to do, He read from Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim freedom for the prisoners and recovery of sight for the blind, to set the oppressed free” (Luke 4:18).

He said He came so people “may have life, and have it to the full” (John 10:10). He fed people who were hungry and healed people who were sick, and He never treated those things as a distraction from the real work. They were the work.

And when He described the final judgment in Matthew 25, the question wasn’t what we believed in the abstract. It was whether we fed the hungry, welcomed the stranger, cared for the sick and visited the prisoner. “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.”

The prophets were just as blunt. In Isaiah 58, God tells people who are very good at religious activity that the worship He wants is “to share your food with the hungry and to provide the poor wanderer with shelter.” Micah boils it down to three things: act justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God.

So we don’t pursue justice because we feel guilty, or because it’s trending, or because it makes us look like good people. We do it because we follow Jesus, and this is where He goes.

A whole-life ethic

From the start, Reject Apathy has been built on what we call a whole-life ethic. It’s the belief that every life is created by God, has a purpose and should be given the opportunity to live fully.

“Pro-life” has become a narrow term in American life. I think it should be much bigger. If human life is sacred, it’s sacred everywhere and at every stage: “from the womb to the cradle to the wheelchair to the grave,” as we put it in 2013. It’s sacred in a delivery room in rural Nigeria and in a refugee camp and in a neighborhood ten minutes from your house.

That’s a consistent ethic, and it doesn’t fit neatly into either political party. We’re fine with that. It means some of what we publish will make conservatives uncomfortable and some will make progressives uncomfortable. We’re not trying to score points. We’re trying to take seriously the idea that every person bears God’s image, and follow that wherever it leads.

The five things we’ll cover

A whole-life ethic needs somewhere to land. Since the first issue, Reject Apathy has focused on five areas where human life is most often threatened. We’re keeping all five.

  • Defense of innocent lives. Children, the unborn, trafficking victims, refugees, people persecuted for their faith. Scripture tells us to “speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves” (Proverbs 31:8). These are the people with the least power to protect themselves, and they are who God consistently tells His people to protect.
  • Preventable disease. “Preventable” is a word charged with hope. It means the knowledge, the medicine and the tools already exist. Mothers still die in childbirth and children still die of malaria, pneumonia and unclean water, not because we don’t know how to stop it, but because the solutions haven’t reached them yet. This is one of the places where a generation can save lives in measurable numbers, and you’ll see us return to it often.
  • Systemic poverty. Poverty is about more than money. It’s a lack of options, and often a lack of dignity. Trace most of the world’s injustice back far enough and you’ll find it. We’ll cover what keeps people trapped and, just as much, what is helping them get free.
  • Violence. War, conflict, abuse and the people caught in the middle of it. Christians land in different places on questions of war and peace, and we won’t pretend otherwise. But we can all stand with the victims, and we all follow the One who said, “Blessed are the peacemakers.”
  • Creation care. “The earth is the Lord’s, and everything in it” (Psalm 24:1). We aren’t going to cover climate data for its own sake. We’re going to cover what happens to people. When droughts lengthen, storms intensify and land stops producing food, it’s the poor who are hit first and hardest. Families lose their livelihoods and their homes. Caring for what God made is a way of caring for the people who depend on it. That makes it a life issue.

These five aren’t separate causes competing for your attention. They’re connected. Poverty feeds disease. Environmental collapse feeds displacement. Displacement feeds violence and exploitation. Pull on one thread and the others move. That’s why we cover them together.

Doing justice the right way

Good intentions aren’t enough. History is full of people who rushed in to help with the best possible motives and left things worse, damaging a culture or creating dependence. We said in the first issue that we were “very aware that our help can sometimes hurt,” and that’s still true.

So we committed to a few principles then, and we’re recommitting to them now.

We’ll favor sustainable solutions over quick fixes. We’ll highlight local leadership, because it’s arrogant to think we have all the answers. Lasting change comes from the people closest to the problem. We’ll look for transparency in the organizations we point you to. We’ll take the long view, because cycles of poverty and violence that took generations to build don’t break in a news cycle.

And we’ll keep faith at the center. A full stomach matters. So does the soul of the person being fed. We believe real, lasting renewal is rooted in Christ.

Here’s what that means for the journalism. Each week’s story will be reported, not just opined about. We’ll talk to people doing the work and people living the reality. We’ll get the facts right and show our sources. We won’t sensationalize suffering, and we won’t flatten complicated situations into partisan talking points. We want you to finish a Reject Apathy story understanding something you didn’t before.

What we’ll ask of you

Awareness that doesn’t lead anywhere is how we all got numb in the first place. So every story will end with a way to respond. Sometimes that will mean using your voice: bringing an issue to your church, your campus, your small group, your corner of the internet. Sometimes it will mean giving your time to an organization in your own city. Sometimes it will mean giving your resources to people on the front lines who know exactly what to do with them.

It won’t look the same every week, because the issues aren’t the same. A story about foster care in America calls for something different than a story about maternal health in South Sudan. We’ll point you to the response that fits, and to organizations we’ve vetted.

You are not being asked to carry all of it. Nobody can. Frederick Buechner wrote that the place God calls you to is where your deep gladness and the world’s deep hunger meet. Our hope is that somewhere in these stories, over the coming weeks and months, you find that place. One issue that won’t let go of you. One thing you can do, and then keep doing.

It is possible

I want to end with the same line we ended on in the first issue of Reject Apathy, because I believe it more now than I did then.

We wrote that our prayer for these stories was that readers would “see it is possible to change the world. It is possible to make a difference. It is possible to reject apathy.”

There is plenty of evidence for that hope. Diseases that once killed millions have been pushed to the edge of eradication within our lifetimes. Communities written off as hopeless have been rebuilt by the people who live in them. None of it happened because someone felt bad for a moment and scrolled on. It happened because ordinary people decided the suffering of someone they would never meet was their concern, and then they stayed with it.

We aren’t going to save the world. That’s Jesus’ job, and He’s already at work. Ours is to be faithful: to see clearly, to care honestly and to show up. This generation is the most connected, most informed generation of Christians in history. We know more about our global neighbors than any believers before us. The only question is what we’ll do with it.

We’ll see you Thursdays.

items.title: The Invitation Has Been Offered
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our Gospel today is the parable of the wedding banquet, and like all the parables, it’s kind of unsettling.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our Gospel today is the parable of the wedding banquet, and like all the parables, it’s kind of unsettling. What we’re meant to see is that this invitation from the king is the greatest invitation possible. God the Father is asking you, personally, to come to the marriage feast for his son. Therefore, the refusal to accept that offer is the central tragedy of the spiritual life. Will you say yes to God’s invitation? And not only that, but will you behave as someone who is worthy of being in God’s house?

Daily Reading

First Reading
Isaiah 25:6-10a

In this mountain the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples
    a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wines,
    of rich food filled with marrow, of well-aged wines strained clear.
And he will destroy on this mountain
    the shroud that is cast over all peoples,
    the sheet that is spread over all nations;
    he will swallow up death forever.
Then the Lord God will wipe away the tears from all faces,
    and the disgrace of his people he will take away from all the earth,
    for the Lord has spoken.
It will be said on that day,
    Lo, this is our God; we have waited for him, so that he might save us.
    This is the Lord for whom we have waited;
    let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation.
For the hand of the Lord will rest on this mountain.

The Moabites shall be trodden down in their place
    as straw is trodden down in a dung-pit.

Psalm
Psalm 23:1-3a, 3b-4, 5, 6

The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want.
    He makes me lie down in green pastures;
he leads me beside still waters;
    he restores my soul.
He leads me in right paths
    for his name’s sake.
Even though I walk through the darkest valley,
    I fear no evil;
for you are with me;
    your rod and your staff—
    they comfort me.
You prepare a table before me
    in the presence of my enemies;
you anoint my head with oil;
    my cup overflows.
Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me
    all the days of my life,
and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord
    my whole life long.

Second Reading
Philippians 4:12-14, 19-20

I know what it is to have little, and I know what it is to have plenty. In any and all circumstances I have learned the secret of being well-fed and of going hungry, of having plenty and of being in need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me. In any case, it was kind of you to share my distress.

And my God will fully satisfy every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 22:1-14

Once more Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying: “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding banquet for his son. He sent his slaves to call those who had been invited to the wedding banquet, but they would not come. Again he sent other slaves, saying, ‘Tell those who have been invited: Look, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready; come to the wedding banquet.’ But they made light of it and went away, one to his farm, another to his business, while the rest seized his slaves, mistreated them, and killed them. The king was enraged. He sent his troops, destroyed those murderers, and burned their city. Then he said to his slaves, ‘The wedding is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go therefore into the main streets, and invite everyone you find to the wedding banquet.’ Those slaves went out into the streets and gathered all whom they found, both good and bad; so the wedding hall was filled with guests.

“But when the king came in to see the guests, he noticed a man there who was not wearing a wedding robe, and he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding robe?’ And he was speechless. Then the king said to the attendants, ‘Bind him hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ For many are called, but few are chosen.”

items.title: Recent Ratzingeria: A Scholar’s Top 10 Benedict XVI Reads
items.author: Dr. Tracey Rowland
items.summary:
Dr. Tracey Rowland

The following are the top ten publications of significant reference works that primarily deal with Ratzinger’s fundamental theology.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tracey Rowland

The year 2027 will mark the centenary of the birth of Joseph Ratzinger and celebrations—mostly in the form of academic conferences or musical soirees—are planned throughout the world. In the Anglosphere, the celebrations will also be spurred on by the publication of significant reference works that mostly deal with Ratzinger’s fundamental theology. They include the following:

  1. Joseph Ratzinger in Dialogue with Philosophical Traditions, Vol 1: From Plato to Vattimo, and Joseph Ratzinger in Dialogue with Philosophical Traditions, Vol II: From Aristotle to Žižek, edited by Alejandro Sado, Rudy Albino de Assunção, and Tracey Rowland. (London: Bloomsbury, 2025 and 2026).

Each volume contains essays by an international team of scholars who examine Ratzinger’s engagement with over twenty different philosophers and/or philosophical traditions. Taken together, these volumes cover some forty different philosophers and traditions whose names and ideas appear in Ratzinger’s publications. These essays are invaluable for understanding the relationship between faith and reason in Ratzinger’s theology.

  1. The Inspiration and Truth of Scripture: Testing the Ratzinger Paradigm (Catholic University of America Press, 2023), by Aaron Pidel, SJ. 

This work offers a synthetic account of Ratzinger’s approach to scriptural theology in juxtaposition to three alternative approaches. The three alternatives are those of Pierre Benoit, Karl Rahner, and David Tracy. Pidel calls Benoit’s approach the Thomist-instrumental model, Rahner’s approach the Molinist-predefinitive model, Tracy’s approach the Heideggerian-disclosive model, and Ratzinger’s approach the Bonaventurian-ecclesial model. The first word in each model’s hyphenated name designates a school of thought, the second word is the way by which God becomes a true “author” of Scripture. Ratzinger’s approach comes closest to Tracy’s disclosive model, but Ratzinger and Tracy differ on the nature of the truth disclosed and the nature of the subjectivity receiving the disclosure. Heidegger’s disclosure model of truth requires one to adopt the right prejudice and thus the nature of the subject receiving the disclosure becomes very important. In Ratzinger’s thought, the Church—understood as the people of God—is the receiving subject. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Fr. Pidel further argues that this approach of Ratzinger incorporates the strengths of the other three models, along with insights from St. Bonaventure, St. John Henry Newman, Romano Guardini, and Erich Przywara. 

Fr. Pidel’s book is likely to become the classical understanding of Ratzinger’s approach to scriptural exegesis and more broadly, the Scripture and tradition relationship.

  1. The much-awaited The Joseph Ratzinger Compendium (Ignatius Press, autumn 2026). 

This is a collection of 104 essays written by seventy-two scholars. Each essay addresses one topic in the theology of Ratzinger. The essays are approximately 4,000 words in length and supported with a bibliography. The first edition of the Compendium will be in English, and there are plans for editions in Spanish, German, and Italian. The chief editor is Dr. Rudy Albino de Assunção from Brazil. The late Pope Benedict was made aware of this forthcoming publication before his death, and at the time, he joked about there being seventy-two scholars to summarise his works and seventy-two scholars to translate the Hebrew Pentateuch into Greek. He was amused by this fact that had never occurred to the editors.

  1. The Oxford Handbook of Joseph Ratzinger, edited by Tracey Rowland and Francesca Aran Murphy (2026).

The Oxford Handbook of Joseph Ratzinger was published in January 2026. It contains twenty-nine essays from an international cohort of scholars. It includes contributions by theologians who worked with Ratzinger during his days as prefect for the Congregation of the Doctrine of the Faith (Don Damiano Marzotto and Don Livio Melina); an essay by Fr. Aaron Pidel on Ratzinger’s understanding of the relationship between the Petrine Office and the Episcopacy, and an essay by Fr. Vincent L. Strand, SJ, on Ratzinger’s theology of priesthood. There are also contributions from two of the leading Ratzinger scholars from Africa: Fr. Maurice Agbaw-Ebai on “Ratzinger and the Johannine Concept of Logos” and Fr. Martin Ifeanyi Onuoha on “The Mariology of Joseph Ratzinger.” The 2024 Ratzinger Prize winner Cyril O’Regan contributed a chapter on Ratzinger’s Principles of Fundamental Theology and Fr. Emery de Gaál addressed the document Dominus Iesus. These are just some of the highlights of this collection.

  1. The Cambridge Companion to Joseph Ratzinger (Cambridge University Press, 2024), edited by Daniel Cardó and Uwe Michael Lang.

The fact that both Oxford and Cambridge University Presses have published handbooks or companions to the thought of Ratzinger speaks volumes about the late pontiff’s standing in the world of theology. There is so much that can be said that the two volumes are not, for the most part, ploughing the same fields and can be read as companions to each other. The Cambridge Companion offers twenty-one essays, including contributions from such luminaries as Bishop Rudolf Voderholzer whom Benedict XVI appointed to the See of Regensburg, Thomas Joseph White, OP, the Rector Magnificus of the Angelicum, Kurt Cardinal Koch, and Fr. Thomas Weinandy, OFM Cap.

  1. The Bloomsbury series T&T Clark Studies in Ressourcement Catholic Theology and Culture has published several works about Ratzinger.
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Fr. Gregory Morgan’s Natural Law & the Secular Mythos (2025) will resonate well with people who share Ratzinger’s approach to the faith and reason, and nature and grace relationships. David Collit’s Hope and History: The Communio and Concilium Alternatives (2026) juxtaposes approaches to the theology of history found in the works of Josef Pieper and Joseph Ratzinger and those found in the theology of Johann Baptist Metz and Walter Kasper. Isabel Troconis’s Ontological and Historical Dimensions of Salvation According to Joseph Ratzinger (2025) examines the history and ontology relationship in the theological anthropology of Ratzinger, while Tomasz Dekert’s Liturgical Peace, Liturgical War: Benedict XVI’s Summorum Pontificum and Its Critics (2025) is focused on Ratzinger’s liturgical theology.

  1. John Henry Newman and Joseph Ratzinger: A Theological Encounter (Washington DC: Catholic University of America Press, 2025). 

This is a collection of conference papers edited by Matthew Levering and Emery de Gaál. Each of the chapters showcases the intellectual affinities between Ratzinger and Newman. A similar collection on Ratzinger and Rahner showcasing the dissimilarities, collated by the same editors, will be published late 2026 or early 2027. 

  1. The Lord Holds Us by the Hand: Private Homilies, Seasons and Feasts (Ignatius Press, 2026).

This is a collection of homilies delivered by Pope Benedict XVI in private chapels and have not, therefore, been in the public domain before this publication.

  1. Beyond the Crisis in the Church: The Pontificate of Benedict XVI (St. Augustine’s Press, 2024) by Roberto Regoli.

Roberto Regoli is the director of the Department of Church History and professor at the Pontifical Gregorian University and president of the Ratzinger Foundation. This work is not an exposition of Ratzinger’s theological teaching but a history of his papacy. It offers a deep-dive into the goings-on inside the Curia during the papacy of Benedict XVI. Significant observations include the intellectual affinity of Ratzinger and Newman and the role of Tarcisio Bertone, the Secretary of State, in the politics of the era.

  1. The Mind of Benedict XVI: A Theology of Communion by Richard G. DeClue, Jr. (Word on Fire, 2024).

Richard DeClue offers a presentation of themes in the fundamental theology of Ratzinger, such as his account of the Trinity, Christology, revelation, and creation in such a way that the coherence of Ratzinger’s theological building-blocks shines forth. The concept of Communion is central to this coherence.

Finally, in addition to this top-ten list, when it comes to identifying circles of interest in Ratzinger studies, the countries of Central Europe have produced prominent scholars of Ratzinger’s thought.The Collected Works of Ratzinger have been published in Polish under the direction of Fr. Krzysztof Góźdź, who is a professor of dogmatic theology at the Catholic University of Lublin (KUL). Tibor Görföl from the University of Pécs has started the work of the translation of the Collected Works into Hungarian, and Alin Tat, a Greek Catholic theologian in the city of Cluj-Napoca (formerly Kolozsvár) in Romania, has translated numerous articles by and about Ratzinger into Romanian.
